target_customer: Muslim retail investors who want Shariah-compliant stock and fund exposure inside their own brokerage account
problem: Shariah compliance depends on complex financial screens that change over time, so Muslim investors struggle to know which stocks and funds they can hold. Amal says it also screens funds, not only stocks.
business_model: One-time access fee for portfolio and screening tools ($249 Standard or $999 Pro per the company site), assets held at the user's own broker
product_category: Halal investing and Shariah screening app

founders.name: Yazin Alirhayim
prior_employers: GE (several years, including about two years as a field engineer installing turbine monitoring equipment)
previous_startups: White (described as Stripe for the Middle East, acquired 2015)
founders.background_notes: Education not stated on the YC page. About 8 years in fintech per YC page.

competitors.name: Wahed Invest
competitors.funding_then: $8M raise in 2018 reported at a $100M valuation, and later rounds before 2022

technical_complexity.rationale: Screening data feeds and a brokerage integration layer with Trading 212 or Alpaca; the hard part is the Shariah methodology and licensed data rather than novel engineering.

defensibility.rationale: Shariah certification from Amanah Advisors adds some trust, but screens and fund rebuilding are copyable by screeners like Zoya or Musaffa and by Wahed.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No acquisition or copy event found in searches through 2025; screening rivals still operate separately.

market_need_then: Muslim investors avoid non-compliant holdings and compliance changes over time; Wahed raised tens of millions by 2020 and 2022 showing paying demand for halal investing. The founder frames the pain as the difficulty of screening funds.

branding.domain_note: Uses amalinvest.com, a descriptive suffix domain; acquisition history not found.

identity.logo: Not described by any source opened
identity.voice_and_tone: Faith-and-values positioning; site stresses Shariah certificate and screening against Israeli military links and boycott lists

brand_strength.rationale: Little press about the brand itself found; the name is an Arabic word (meaning hope per a Wikipedia entry on the given name) but no source ties it to the company, and the value proposition rather than the brand carries it.

outcome_analysis: Amal Invest remains active with a tiny team and no verified outside funding. The founder has prior fintech exits and the product targets a faith-based niche with clear demand, but no source confirms scale, revenue or a priced round, so the trajectory is unknown rather than good or bad. A one-time fee model suggests a capital-light approach.
notes: Funding unverified: Latka lists $0 raised and bootstrapped; another profile lists $500,000 convertible note. Both are single aggregator listings, so no round is recorded. Wahed entry dated 2018 because later round sources were not opened; Zoya and Musaffa found only in 2025 to 2026 sources so not listed. Education not found. Company site did not state founders.
